title: And I Pray
opening: What happens when we pray and pray, yet nothing seems to change? When the burdens of life begin to occupy our thoughts so completely that we struggle to recognize God's presence? Perhaps the question is not simply whether God is listening, but whether we can still make room to hear Him.
body:
Today's first reading from Revelation describes John being instructed to take a small scroll from an angel and eat it. He is told that it will taste sweet as honey but become bitter in his stomach. And that is exactly what happens. Then John receives another instruction: he must prophesy again about many peoples, nations, languages, and kings. I found myself wondering who was speaking to him and what he was being asked to proclaim. As Revelation continues, John is shown more of humanity's struggles, the opposition to God, the suffering of the faithful, and the ultimate victory of God's Kingdom. Receiving God's word was not the end of his responsibility. It was the beginning of something more.

The sweetness and bitterness of the scroll stayed with me. God's word is beautiful to receive. His promises offer hope, His love brings comfort, and His teachings provide a path toward the life He desires for us. But living that word can be difficult. Sometimes the truth challenges us. Sometimes our circumstances seem so far removed from the peace we believe God offers that we struggle to understand what He is asking of us. Perhaps the bitterness is not always in the word itself, but in what we experience as we try to live faithfully in a world that often seems indifferent to what is right.

In today's Gospel, Jesus enters the Temple in Jerusalem and drives out those who are selling things. He declares, “My house shall be a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves.” He then remains in the Temple, teaching each day, while the religious authorities seek a way to put Him to death. Yet they cannot find an opportunity because the people are hanging on His words.

That last detail made me curious. If the people were so captivated by Jesus, what changed? Later, we read of a crowd calling for His crucifixion, although Scripture does not tell us that these were necessarily the same people who had listened to Him in the Temple. Still, it made me think about how easily we can be moved by God's word, yet struggle to remain faithful to it when life becomes difficult. We may welcome what comforts us, but find it harder to accept what challenges us.

And then I began thinking about the Temple itself. Jesus was speaking of His Father's house, a sacred place intended for prayer. But Scripture also teaches that we are temples of the Holy Spirit. If Christ entered the temple of my heart today, what would He find?

I would like to believe He would find a heart filled with love, gratitude, and trust. But lately, I suspect He would also find a great deal of worry, disappointment, frustration, and fear. Life has presented challenges that seem to have no resolution. There are times when I feel I am continually asking for fairness, compassion, and help, only to encounter another obstacle. I pray for guidance and relief, yet the difficulties remain. And somewhere along the way, I have begun to question whether God is listening at all.

That is a difficult thing to admit, especially when I know how deeply I want to believe in His love.

I have also begun questioning myself. Why am I so consumed with my own problems? Why do my worries occupy so much of my attention? Am I becoming selfish, or expecting more than I should? I don't believe that asking for justice or relief is wrong, but I recognize how easily these struggles can take over my thoughts. They begin to occupy the very space where I want God to dwell.

And perhaps that is what I find so meaningful about Jesus cleansing the Temple. He does not abandon it because its purpose has been compromised. He enters it, confronts what does not belong, and restores it as a place of prayer. He remains there teaching.

I want Jesus to do that within me.

Not because I believe every worry or doubt is sinful, or because I think He is disappointed in me for struggling. I want Him to help me recognize what is taking hold of my heart and preventing me from experiencing the love and peace I seek in Him. I want Him to reclaim the space that fear and disappointment have occupied, to help me release what I cannot control, and to guide me through what still requires my attention.

But there is something more. As I considered what I wanted Jesus to drive out of my heart, I realized that perhaps what I need most is simply for Him to enter and remain with me.

I have been asking Him to help me with so many things. And when those prayers seem unanswered, I begin to feel rejected, as though I have been left alone to fight battles I no longer have the strength to fight. I know that feeling abandoned does not necessarily mean I have been abandoned. Yet knowing that does not always remove the sorrow.

I think of yesterday's Gospel, when Jesus approached Jerusalem and wept. He knew the suffering that was coming, and His response was sorrow. Today, He enters the Temple and restores its purpose. There is something deeply comforting in the thought that Christ does not turn away from what is troubled. He comes near, even when His presence is not welcomed by everyone.

Perhaps that is what I need to remember when I struggle to recognize Him in my own life.

And I return to John's scroll. It was sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach, yet he was told to continue. His experience was part of a prophetic calling, but it also invites me to reflect upon my own faith. I know the sweetness of God's love and promises. I also know the bitterness of disappointment and uncertainty. I cannot always reconcile the two, and perhaps I do not have to understand everything before I can continue seeking Him.

I don't want my relationship with God to become defined by what He has or has not done for me. I want to know Him, to love Him, and to allow His love to shape the way I live. I want to recognize the gifts of the Holy Spirit, to be guided by His wisdom, and to make room in my heart for the needs of others, even while I am struggling with my own.

That does not mean ignoring injustice or pretending that life's difficulties do not matter. It means remembering that my problems, however consuming they may feel, are not the entirety of my life or my relationship with God.

Jesus said His Father's house shall be a house of prayer. Perhaps the same invitation extends to the temple of our hearts. Not that we must arrive before Him without fear, sorrow, or doubt, but that we allow Him to enter those places and restore our attention to what matters most.

I cannot always hear God's voice above the noise of my worries. I cannot always recognize His presence when life becomes difficult. And I cannot honestly say that I understand why some prayers seem to go unanswered.

But I know that I want Him here.

I want Him to reclaim what fear and disappointment have taken from my heart. I want Him to restore it as a place where His love can dwell freely, where I can learn to listen, and where my faith is not measured only by the circumstances of my life.

I do not know when relief will come. I do not know what tomorrow will bring. But I know who I want as my companion along the way.

And I pray.
prayer: Heavenly Father,  Your word is sweet, filled with promises of love, mercy, and hope. Yet there are times when life feels bitter, when my prayers seem unanswered, and when I struggle to recognize Your presence.  Lord Jesus, enter the temple of my heart. Reclaim what belongs to You. Help me recognize the worries, fears, and disappointments that have occupied so much of my thoughts. Teach me to seek what is right without allowing frustration to consume me, and to face life's difficulties without losing sight of Your love.  Holy Spirit, guide me with Your wisdom and understanding. Help me recognize the gifts You have given me and the opportunities to share Your love with others. When I become consumed by my own struggles, gently turn my attention toward You and toward those who may also be suffering.  And Lord, when I feel alone, when I wonder whether You are listening, please help me remain open to Your presence. I do not need to understand everything today. I simply ask that You remain with me and help me recognize You in the midst of it all.  Make my heart a house of prayer, a place where Your love can grow, where my worries do not silence my faith, and where I can continue to seek You even when the answers do not come.  And I pray, Lord, because above all else, it is You I want.  Amen.
scripture: Revelation 10:8–11; Psalm 119:14, 24, 72, 103, 111, 131; Luke 19:45–48; 1 Corinthians 3:16; Psalm 13:2–6; Psalm 22:2; Matthew 27:46.
theme: When the sweetness of faith meets the bitterness of life, and we begin to question whether God is listening
